comparison_rules.pet_vs_pet_wool: PET Wool is lower density and more porous, so it generally absorbs more sound at a given thickness. High-density PET has a higher fire rating (EN-13501 Class B vs C) and additional fire test certifications (ASTM D 2859, BS 5852 Part 1), making it preferred where stricter fire safety is required.
comparison_rules.flat_vs_embossed: Flat panels absorb more sound at comparable thickness because their full surface area is exposed to incoming sound. Embossed panels trade some absorption for partial diffusion and architectural surface relief — they are selected when visual depth and sculptural character matter alongside acoustic function.
comparison_rules.thickness_effect: Thicker panels absorb lower frequencies and deliver higher overall NRC. Example: PET Wool flat goes from NRC 0.70 at 20 mm to NRC 0.90 at 40 mm.
comparison_rules.backing_effect: Adding an air gap or infill behind the panel effectively increases the absorbing layer and can lift NRC up to 0.80–0.90, especially in the low-to-mid frequency range.
comparison_rules.highest_nrc_product: Flat Panel VMT (PET Wool) 40 mm at NRC 0.90 (direct fix).
comparison_rules.best_for_print: Flat Panel VMT (PET) — high-density surface supports refined high-resolution printing. Flat Panel VMT (PET Wool) also supports high-resolution printing.
comparison_rules.best_for_sculptural_design: Embossed VMT series (either PET or PET Wool) — sculpted relief adds architectural depth.

acoustics_general_knowledge.nrc_definition: Noise Reduction Coefficient (NRC) is the average sound absorption coefficient at 250, 500, 1000, and 2000 Hz. Values range from 0 (perfect reflector) to 1 (perfect absorber). A panel with NRC 0.70 absorbs about 70% of incident sound across those frequencies.
acoustics_general_knowledge.alpha_w_definition: αw (weighted sound absorption coefficient, per ISO 11654) is a single-number rating derived from the 1/3-octave absorption curve by fitting it against a reference curve. It ranges from 0 to 1 (values above 1 in lab measurements reflect edge-diffraction effects in the test chamber and are typically reported as 1.00 in specifications).
acoustics_general_knowledge.nrc_vs_alpha_w: NRC is the ASTM/North American standard; αw is the ISO/European equivalent. UniVicoustic reports both on its data sheets because specifications cited in projects use either system.
acoustics_general_knowledge.absorption_vs_soundproofing: Absorption reduces reverberation and echo *inside* a room by converting sound energy into heat within porous material. Soundproofing (sound isolation) prevents sound from *passing through* a wall into another space and requires mass, decoupling, damping, and airtight sealing. Acoustic panels like these are absorbers, not soundproofing.
acoustics_general_knowledge.frequency_coverage: PET and PET Wool fibre panels are primarily effective at mid-to-high frequencies (roughly 500 Hz and above). Low-frequency absorption improves with greater panel thickness and rear air gap.
acoustics_general_knowledge.air_gap_rule_of_thumb: A rear air gap roughly equal to one-quarter wavelength of the target frequency improves absorption at that frequency. Practical gaps of 25–50 mm noticeably improve mid-frequency absorption.
acoustics_general_knowledge.room_coverage_rule_of_thumb: For general reverberation control in speech spaces, treating 15–30% of total room surface area (walls + ceiling) with an NRC 0.7+ product is a common starting point. Music, home theatre, and broadcast spaces usually need more. A proper calculation uses Sabine's formula based on room volume and target reverberation time.
